title: Flour costs $2 more. Does bread?
hook: Flour adds $2 to the cost of every loaf. How much does the price of bread rise?

knows: the bread market model: buyers' line, bakers' line, price where they cross (supply-demand lesson)
doesNotKnow: that a cost rise shifts the whole supply line, not just the price
that buyers buy less, so the price rises by less than the cost

misconception: If flour costs more, bread should cost exactly that much more.
objective: The learner can explain that a cost rise moves the whole supply line, that the new price is where it meets demand again, and that because buyers cut back the price rises by less than the cost in this model.

claims.text: With buyers wanting 100 − 10p loaves and bakers baking 10p − 20, the price is $6 and 40 loaves sell.
If flour adds $2 to each loaf's cost, bakers bake 10p − 40, and the new price is $7 with 30 loaves.
At $8 buyers would want only 20 loaves while bakers would bake 40, so loaves would go unsold.
On the stage the price rises by half the added cost (for example $1 of flour gives $6.50 and 35 loaves), because the two lines are equally steep.
claims.source: eqPrice(c) = 6 + c/2; q = 40 − 5c. In quantity-per-dollar slopes, the share passed on = supply slope / (supply slope + demand slope) = 10/(10 + 10) = 1/2 (in price-per-loaf slopes it is demand slope / (supply slope + demand slope), also 1/2 here) (Mankiw, Principles of Economics, ch. 6, tax incidence uses the same algebra). | CLAIM FIX 2026-10-13: Source note only: the general pass-through rule was stated backwards for price-per-loaf slopes. Now stated in quantity-per-dollar slopes (10/(10+10)) with the price-slope form d/(s+d) added. Claim text and stage numbers unchanged.

claims.text: After a $2 flour rise, buyers pay $1 more and bakers keep $5 a loaf after the extra cost instead of $6.
The lesson is a toy model: straight lines, one market; how much of a real cost rise reaches prices varies.
claims.source: Assumptions of the lesson's own calculation, shown on the stage chip and in the reveal.

recall.question: A coffee bean shortage adds $1 to the cost of every cup. In a market where buyers cut back when prices rise, what happens to the price of a cup?
recall.why: The cost rise shifts the whole supply line up by $1. Buyers buy fewer cups at a higher price, so the new crossing is less than $1 higher: buyers and sellers share the cost.
